learningObjective: Explain the graph-coloring formulation of register allocation, including the meaning of interference and spilling.

canonicalClaims.claim: Chaitin/Briggs-style register allocation models virtual registers (live ranges) as graph nodes, adds an edge between two live ranges when they are simultaneously live (interfere), and colors the graph with K colors corresponding to K physical registers; when a K-coloring fails, one or more live ranges are spilled to memory.
conditions: Target has K physical registers of the relevant class.
Live ranges are computed via liveness analysis; interference is derived from concurrent liveness.
nonImplications: Does not imply graph coloring is the only algorithm; linear-scan (LLVM), PBQP, and SSA-based allocators are alternatives.
Does not imply spilling causes uniform slowdown; live-range splitting can localize memory access.

misconceptions.claim: Graph coloring register allocation operates on basic blocks, not live ranges.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Nodes are live ranges (virtual registers); basic blocks are units of the CFG, not the interference graph.

misconceptions.claim: SSA phi nodes are the units colored by the register allocator.
misconceptions.whyWrong: SSA is typically destructed to explicit copies before allocation; the allocator operates on live ranges.

misconceptions.claim: Register allocation and instruction scheduling are the same problem.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Register allocation assigns storage; scheduling reorders instructions to hide latency and fill functional units. They interact but are distinct passes.

implementationFacts: Chaitin: simplify (remove degree < K), then color; if a degree ≥ K node remains, spill.
Briggs: optimistic coloring; try to color after simplifying even high-degree nodes.
LLVM's default allocator is greedy linear-scan-derived, not pure graph coloring.
performanceScenarios: High register-pressure kernels (large fused kernels, unrolled loops) exercise the allocator heavily; excessive spilling manifests as many loads/stores in the emitted code.
